edition.deck: A US president signals a possible immigration rethink after election losses, while courts, public services and security concerns shape the day’s agenda.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises fresh developments and consequential reporting. Continuing stories appear only where this gather adds a meaningful update or distinct reporting.

content.headline: Trump says immigration crackdown was too tough after midterm losses
content.shortHeadline: Trump says immigration crackdown was too tough
content.standfirst: The president says mass deportations hurt Republicans at the polls and suggests a deal with Democrats could let some long-term undocumented residents stay. His administration says enforcement will continue.

image.caption: Donald Trump says his immigration policy may have been too tough.

sources.originalTitle: Trump says immigration crackdown was 'too tough' and played part in midterms defeat
Trump tells 60 Minutes that deportation policy was ‘too tough’

segments.body: Donald Trump said his immigration crackdown was “too tough” in an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes, acknowledging that deportations had politically hurt Republicans after their midterm losses. He said he would be open to working with Democrats on immigration but offered no detailed plan in the BBC’s account.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that Trump floated a deal for some long-term undocumented residents who work and pay taxes, while continuing to deport people convicted of serious crimes. It also describes the effects of the crackdown on families and immigrant communities.

segments.title: A change in tone, not yet in policy
segments.body: Trump said he would like to “do something on immigration” with Democrats, but the Department of Homeland Security said it was not slowing arrests or deportations. His promotion of Stephen Miller, a leading architect of the hardline policy, also contrasts with the conciliatory tone of the interview.

content.headline: At least seven killed and more than 100 injured in Egypt train crash
content.shortHeadline: Egypt train crash kills at least seven and injures more than 100
content.standfirst: Two trains collided near Giza, derailing carriages and prompting an emergency response. The public prosecutor has warned the death toll could rise; the cause has not been established.

image.caption: Derailed train carriages at the crash site near Giza, Egypt.

sources.originalTitle: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt

segments.body: At least seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two trains collided near Giza, south of Cairo, according to Egyptian authorities. Several carriages derailed and fell down an embankment. The driver of one train was among those killed, and the public prosecutor said the death toll could rise.

The first train, travelling from Giza to Fayoum, struck the rear of a stationary train heading from Cairo to Aswan. Hospitals were placed on heightened alert and services between Giza and Upper Egypt were suspended while cranes were sent to remove the wreckage. Authorities have not said how long disruption will last or what caused the collision.

content.headline: Kraków shooting investigated as terrorism after six killed
content.shortHeadline: Kraków shooting: six killed as police pursue terror inquiry
content.standfirst: Two officers injured while stopping the gunman have emerged from comas. Investigators are examining possible far-right links, while the attacker remains in critical condition and his family were also found dead.

image.caption: Surgeon Michal Pędziwiatr describes treating victims after the Kraków shooting.

sources.originalTitle: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague says
To læger spiste frokost tæt på skyderiet i Kraków: 'Vi besluttede os for at hjælpe ofrene så hurtigt som muligt'

segments.body: Six people were killed in Saturday’s shooting in central Kraków. The BBC reports 15 people were injured; DR’s account gives 16, including the suspected gunman. Poland’s prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation, and officials have said the 24-year-old suspect may have been influenced by far-right ideology.

perspectives.body: DR reports that the suspect’s parents and sister were found shot dead at his home. It says authorities have not established his motive or whether anyone else knew of his plans.

segments.title: People who ran towards the gunfire
segments.body: Surgeons Michal Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch nearby when the shooting began. They treated injured people before ambulances arrived, including a badly wounded police officer. Pędziwiatr said they also treated the suspected attacker as a patient.

content.headline: Gadi Eisenkot seeks coalition partners after receiving mandate in Israel
content.shortHeadline: Eisenkot begins talks to form Israel’s next government
content.standfirst: The former military chief has 28 days to find the votes to govern, despite neither bloc winning a majority. He is reaching out to Netanyahu’s allies, while possible support from Arab-led parties remains contentious within his camp.

image.caption: Reactions in Israel and the Palestinian territories to Eisenkot’s mandate to form a government.

sources.originalTitle: Gadi Eisenkot reaches out to Netanyahu allies as he strives to form government

segments.body: Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, has given opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot 28 days to form a government. His bloc won 48 seats in the 120-member parliament, against 53 for Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp, leaving neither side with a majority. Eisenkot has appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud and far-right allies to join a government led by him.

segments.title: A narrow path to a majority
segments.body: Eisenkot could seek support from Arab-led parties, which endorsed him during consultations with Herzog, but some of his partners oppose such an arrangement. Another option is an agreement with ultra-Orthodox parties, which seek to retain military-service exemptions. If he cannot secure 61 votes, Herzog may grant an extension or ask someone else to try; failure by both sides could lead to another election.

content.headline: Houthis claim fresh strikes on Riyadh as Aramco Tower is damaged
content.shortHeadline: Houthi strikes damage Riyadh tower; Saudi Arabia reports no casualties
content.standfirst: The Saudi energy ministry said the Aramco Tower suffered minor damage, while BBC-authenticated footage showed shattered windows and a badly hit floor. The Houthis also claimed to target the airport and oil facilities.

image.caption: The Aramco Tower in Riyadh was damaged in an attack claimed by the Houthis.

sources.originalTitle: Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes

segments.body: The Aramco Tower in Riyadh’s central financial district was hit in an air attack. The Houthi-controlled Saba news agency said the group had targeted the capital’s business zone, without naming the tower. Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said there was minor damage and no casualties; BBC Verify footage showed damage to several levels.

The Houthis said they also targeted Riyadh airport and Aramco oil-storage facilities; Saudi Arabia said its air defences intercepted several missiles. The claims came amid renewed fighting in Yemen and a breakdown of an informal ceasefire. The two sides have given sharply different accounts of a recent strike in Yemen, and Saudi Arabia has not commented on the Houthi-reported toll there.

content.headline: Wildfires choke Indonesian communities as helicopter crash kills crew member
content.shortHeadline: Indonesia fires bring toxic haze as firefighting helicopter crashes
content.standfirst: Residents in Palangkaraya are relying on volunteer-run clean-air shelters as smoke from fires blankets parts of the region. A helicopter on a firefighting mission crashed in South Kalimantan, killing one crew member; two others were rescued.

image.caption: Apri Dona Yusmelita and her five-month-old son as he receives nebuliser treatment at home in Palangkaraya, Indonesia.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I can’t bear it’: young family takes refuge in bedroom as choking haze engulfs Indonesian city
One killed in Indonesia helicopter crash during firefighting operation

segments.body: Wildfire smoke has left families in Palangkaraya, on Borneo, sheltering in bedrooms and community clean-air rooms. One mother told the Guardian that her infant son has been ill for much of his life; volunteers run 14 haze shelters with air purifiers, oxygen and nebulisers. The report says close to two million hectares of forest and peatland have burned in Indonesia this year.

perspectives.body: Local volunteers are measuring dangerous air pollution, sometimes beyond the range of their monitors. A World Health Organization guideline for average daily PM2.5 is 15 micrograms per cubic metre; readings in Palangkaraya regularly reach 300, the report says.

segments.body: Separately, one Indonesian crew member died when a firefighting helicopter crashed into a river in South Kalimantan. An Australian and a New Zealander were rescued and taken to hospital. Authorities said the crash is under investigation and that firefighting can continue; it came days after another helicopter crash in the region killed three crew members.

content.headline: South Africa’s ANC posts its worst local election result
content.shortHeadline: ANC’s local election vote falls to a record low in South Africa
content.standfirst: The governing party won 30.76% of the vote and a majority in only one province, amid criticism of poor public services. Coalition negotiations now loom in major cities as the party faces a new phase of decline.

image.caption: Voters cast ballots during South Africa’s local government elections in Johannesburg.

sources.originalTitle: South Africa's ANC records worst-ever results in local elections

segments.body: The African National Congress won 30.76% of the vote in South Africa’s local elections, its lowest share in such polls since the end of apartheid. It won a majority in just one of nine provinces and the most votes in two of eight major cities. President Cyril Ramaphosa said the party accepted voters’ verdict; its secretary-general called the result “catastrophic”.

Analysts cited failures in water, power and sanitation as central to the ANC’s decline. The Democratic Alliance finished second nationally, while former president Jacob Zuma’s MK party displaced the ANC as the leading party in Durban. Parties have 14 days to negotiate local coalitions, with Johannesburg and Pretoria among the cities under close scrutiny.

content.headline: Pope Leo urges Argentina’s Milei to put people before the economy
content.shortHeadline: Pope Leo challenges Milei’s austerity drive on Argentina visit
content.standfirst: On his first visit to Argentina as pope, Leo called for growth to benefit everyone and voiced concern for people affected by cuts to disability support. His remarks come as the country remains sharply divided over President Javier Milei’s economic programme.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV shakes hands with Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, in Buenos Aires.

sources.originalTitle: Pope Leo delivers stinging rebuke of Milei’s austerity measures during Argentina visit

segments.body: Pope Leo XIV urged Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, to put people before the economy, saying growth must benefit all. Speaking in Buenos Aires on Sunday, he called for concern for people affected by illness, disability and dependence—an apparent reference to disputed cuts to disability assistance—and urged public officials to listen carefully.

The visit is the first by a pope to Argentina in nearly four decades and comes after three years of austerity under Milei, whose policies have divided the country. Poverty rose to 32.3% in September, the report says. Leo also stressed integrity in public office and is due to visit a home for disabled people and a prison during his tour.

content.headline: Ministers expected to cut UK electric-car sales target despite Labour concerns
content.shortHeadline: UK ministers expected to weaken electric-car sales target
content.standfirst: A cut to the 2030 zero-emission vehicle target is expected this week, with government insiders suggesting a level near 60%. Ministers say no decision has been taken; critics warn a change could undermine climate goals and charging investment.

image.caption: A carmaker’s electric vehicle at an industry event.

sources.originalTitle: Labour expected to cut EV targets for UK’s car industry despite MPs’ protests
Climate always comes second: are green issues slipping down Burnham’s agenda?

segments.body: Ministers are expected to reduce the 2030 target for electric-vehicle sales by about a quarter, with government insiders telling the Guardian that a target of roughly 60% is likely, rather than the current 80%. The government says no decision has been made and maintains its commitment to ending sales of new petrol- and diesel-only cars by 2030.

perspectives.body: Carmakers argue the interim targets are out of reach: battery electric vehicles made up 26.6% of new car sales in the first ten months of this year, against a 33% target. Industry exemptions mean that headline targets do not translate directly into fines for every shortfall.

segments.body: Labour MPs and environmental campaigners say weakening the mandate would put climate commitments and investment at risk. ChargeUK says £1.7bn of charging infrastructure could be exposed to uncertainty. The government’s August consultation included options to reduce the 2030 target to 70%, 60% or 50%, or keep it unchanged with greater flexibility.

content.headline: GPs to offer 300,000 vulnerable patients extra support this winter
content.shortHeadline: £40m GP scheme aims to keep vulnerable patients out of hospital
content.standfirst: A £40m England programme will fund health checks, medication reviews and respiratory tests for people considered at risk of becoming seriously unwell. The Royal College of GPs welcomed the prevention focus but said lasting improvement requires sustained investment.

image.caption: GP practices can use £126 for each eligible patient supported by the winter scheme.

sources.originalTitle: GPs to offer 300,000 patients extra support to ease winter strain on NHS

segments.body: GP practices in England are to offer extra support to 300,000 patients with frailty and long-term conditions, including heart and lung disease. The £40m scheme will fund checks, medication reviews and respiratory tests intended to catch problems early and reduce avoidable hospital visits this winter. The money is being reallocated from existing GP budgets for 2026–27.

Practices can use £126 for each eligible patient supported. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would not pretend winter would be easy and described the programme as part of efforts to keep people well at home. The Royal College of GPs welcomed the focus on prevention but warned that short-term initiatives cannot replace long-term, sustainable investment in general practice.

content.headline: Fewer than one in 15 stroke survivors get recommended rehabilitation
content.shortHeadline: Only 6.4% of stroke survivors receive recommended therapy
content.standfirst: An annual audit found just 6.4% of patients in England, Wales and Northern Ireland received the recommended three hours of daily rehabilitation on five days a week. The Stroke Association says shortages of aftercare are undermining recovery.

image.caption: Almost 100,000 people a year in the UK have a stroke.

sources.originalTitle: Only 6.4% of stroke survivors receive enough therapy, finds ‘damning’ report

segments.body: Only 6.4% of stroke patients in England, Wales and Northern Ireland received the recommended three hours of rehabilitation a day, at least five days a week, in the first quarter of this year. The figure is from the latest Sentinel Stroke National Audit Programme report and is down from 7.5% in late 2024.

Patients received an average of 40 minutes of therapy in the period, and only 68% received ongoing rehabilitation support after leaving hospital. The Stroke Association called the figures “damning”, saying too many survivors lack care during recovery. The Department of Health and Social Care said the NHS was working to provide rapid support and long-term rehabilitation.

content.headline: UK rail cyberattack could cause week of disruption and £1.8bn loss
content.shortHeadline: Rail cyberattack could cost £1.8bn and disrupt services for a week
content.standfirst: Government-commissioned research modelled a low-likelihood attack on rail communications that could paralyse some routes and slow others. Experts warn of vulnerabilities, while the transport department says operators need stronger preparation and testing.

image.caption: The government wants to strengthen the railway’s resilience against cyber threats.

sources.originalTitle: How Putin could bring Britain’s railways to a halt

segments.body: A cyberattack on Network Rail’s train communications could disrupt services for a week and cost the economy £1.8bn, according to government-commissioned KPMG research cited by the i Paper. The scenario includes £281.3m in passenger delays, though researchers assessed its likelihood as low.

Experts said an attack on communications could force services to stop or run at reduced speeds. The Department for Transport’s resilience strategy calls for operators to map vulnerabilities, coordinate stress tests and improve information-sharing. Previous hacks have hit ticketing and station Wi-Fi systems, but have not disrupted train operations.

perspectives.body: The research describes a hypothetical scenario, not an imminent threat assessment. A cyber-security academic quoted by the i Paper nevertheless expects hostile states to try a major attack on UK critical transport infrastructure by 2028.

content.headline: Energy firms could use HMRC data to target future bill support
content.shortHeadline: HMRC income data could help decide who gets energy-bill support
content.standfirst: A proposed law would let government departments share income and other records with energy suppliers for future support schemes. None has been designed yet, and the documents suggest any scheme could mean higher bills for households not eligible for help.

image.caption: The proposed powers are intended to target support to households that need it most.

sources.originalTitle: HMRC could share tax records with energy firms to determine who pays higher bills

segments.body: The Energy Independence Bill would give ministers powers to use government data, including HMRC income records, to identify households for future energy-bill support. No scheme has been designed, and government documents suggest one would not be in place before winter 2028–29 at the earliest.

The government says income data could help reach low-income households missed by schemes based on benefits or property values. The bill’s impact assessment says that if costs are added to energy bills, households not eligible for support—expected to be on higher incomes—could pay more. Departments would not be forced to share data, and further legislation would be needed to establish a scheme.

perspectives.body: The plans are prospective, not a current change to bills or data-sharing. A shadow energy secretary called them “class warfare”; the energy department said claims of privacy overreach were misleading.

content.headline: Foreign Office challenged China over alleged embassy stun weapons
content.shortHeadline: UK confronted China over alleged stun batons at embassy protest
content.standfirst: A minister’s letter says China’s ambassador was told foreign missions must comply with UK law after guards were accused of displaying prohibited electroshock weapons. The police investigation is ongoing and the Chinese embassy has denied the allegations.

image.caption: China’s ambassador was confronted over allegations concerning embassy guards at a London protest.

sources.originalTitle: The UK’s secret row with China over embassy guards carrying electroshock weapons

segments.body: The Foreign Office confronted China’s ambassador, Zheng Zeguang, over allegations that embassy staff brandished electroshock weapons at protesters in London. A letter from security minister Dan Jarvis says the ambassador was told diplomatic missions must follow UK law and that any request for immunity should be waived if police have grounds to interview guards.

The allegations relate to a July protest outside the embassy. Two protesters said a device was pointed at them; witnesses described what they saw as stun batons. The Metropolitan Police said it was reviewing footage. China’s embassy has denied the claims, calling them “fabrication and defamation”, and said activists tried to force their way onto its premises.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reporting is based on a letter from the security minister to a Conservative counterpart. The opposition minister argued the government should have made its response public; no finding of wrongdoing has been reported.

content.headline: Women in comedy still rely on private warnings about alleged abusers
content.shortHeadline: Women comedians say whisper networks persist after Brand conviction
content.standfirst: Female comedians say private messages warning colleagues about men in the industry remain necessary because formal workplace safeguards are lacking. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has urged media organisations to take abuse seriously after Russell Brand’s conviction.

image.caption: Comedian Kate Smurthwaite says women still use private groups to warn one another about men in the industry.

sources.originalTitle: The female comedians who use WhatsApp groups to warn of TV abusers
'Time is up': Minister warns media industry to take abuse seriously in wake of Brand case

segments.body: Female comedians told the i Paper they still use private WhatsApp groups to warn one another about men in the industry after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault. Comedian Kate Smurthwaite said she remains in five or six such groups but does not see them as a solution to what she called a wider cultural problem.

One unnamed high-profile comedian said some male performers were not allowed to be left alone with young women, and argued that employers and men in the industry must take responsibility. In a separate BBC interview, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said many people had approached her with allegations and urged other organisations to join an independent standards body for whistleblowers.

perspectives.body: Nandy said she could not assure the public that abuse was no longer happening in media organisations, and described the cost to women who speak up as “very heavy”. The BBC said it had committed to improve its culture and processes.

content.headline: UK minister studies Denmark’s supported-employment scheme for disabled people
content.shortHeadline: UK looks to Denmark’s flexible jobs scheme for welfare reform
content.standfirst: Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden is examining Denmark’s subsidised jobs for people whose health or disability limits their work. Danish employment rates have risen, but the model involves much higher spending on employment support than the UK currently provides.

image.caption: Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden visits a job centre in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: The Nordic nation the UK wants to model its benefits revamp on – but there’s a catch

segments.body: Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden visited Copenhagen to study Denmark’s Fleksjobs scheme, which subsidises jobs tailored to people’s abilities and can adjust working hours as their needs change. He said he wants Britain’s welfare system to focus more on what people can do and provide “a future, not just an income”.

The i Paper reports that Denmark’s employment rate for disabled people rose from 44% in 2012 to 61% in 2024; the UK rate is about 52%. Danish coaches describe a relationship-led service, with sanctions rare. Denmark spends about 2% of GDP on active labour-market programmes, compared with roughly 0.3% in the UK, raising questions about the cost of adapting the approach.

perspectives.body: The report includes accounts from Danish workers who say flexible jobs helped them regain routine, confidence and a sense of contribution. It also notes that Denmark and the Netherlands spend more on employment and education support than Britain does.

content.headline: Nordea faces verdict in money-laundering case carrying record fine
content.shortHeadline: Nordea awaits verdict in money-laundering case over billions
content.standfirst: Prosecutors are seeking a 6.596bn-kroner fine over alleged money-laundering law breaches from 2012 to 2015. Nordea denies wrongdoing; the court is expected to rule after more than 60 hearings.

image.caption: Nordea’s chief legal officer, Anders Holkmann, speaks to reporters during the case.

source.credit: Foto: Emil Nicolai Helms / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Nu falder dommen over Nordea i historisk sag

segments.body: A verdict is expected Monday in the criminal case against Nordea over alleged breaches of Denmark’s anti-money-laundering law between 2012 and 2015. Prosecutors are seeking a fine of 6.596bn kroner, potentially the largest fine imposed on a bank by Danish authorities. Nordea denies the charges and is seeking acquittal.

The case covers transactions and business worth more than 26bn kroner, including more than 17,000 transfers of nearly 25bn kroner involving 25 high-risk customers, many linked to companies in tax havens with Russian ultimate owners. Prosecutors say the bank failed to monitor customers and report suspicious transactions; Nordea says the rules at the time were unclear and the prosecution has not shown who knew what, or when.

perspectives.body: The central legal question is whether Nordea’s conduct breached the law in force at the time—not whether its systems could have been better by today’s standards. The bank’s defence says the case should not be judged by current expectations.

content.headline: Hotels warn guests after booking-system data breach triggers fake payment claims
content.shortHeadline: Booking-system breach prompts fake payment messages to hotel guests
content.standfirst: Several Danish hotels and Knuthenborg Safaripark say customers have received fraudulent payment requests after a breach at booking-system supplier AK Techotel. Reservation details may have been exposed, but one hotel says payment-card data was not accessed.

image.caption: Hotel Europa in Aabenraa is among the properties affected by the booking-system breach.

sources.originalTitle: Hoteller og turistattraktion ramt af datalæk – tager hændelse "meget alvorligt"

segments.body: Customers at several Danish hotels and Knuthenborg Safaripark have received fake payment requests following a data breach at booking-system provider AK Techotel. The supplier said it was investigating a leak of hotel reservations and that it appeared to involve Denmark only.

A hotel said unauthorised people may have accessed guests’ names, contact details and stay information, but not credit-card data. The businesses warn customers not to click links, reply to messages or enter personal or payment details. AK Techotel’s managing director has not yet commented to TV 2.

content.headline: Temu removes Danish chilled foods after tests find unsafe delivery temperatures
content.shortHeadline: Temu removes chilled foods in Denmark after safety test
content.standfirst: Forbrugerrådet Tænk found that seven tested orders of sausages, pâté and cheese arrived too warm, raising food-safety and labelling concerns. The consumer group advises against buying chilled food through the platform and plans complaints to regulators.

image.caption: Forbrugerrådet Tænk raised food-safety concerns about chilled products ordered through Temu.

sources.originalTitle: Temu-mad risikerer at gøre dig syg, lyder varsel

segments.body: All seven chilled-food orders tested by consumer group Forbrugerrådet Tænk failed its temperature checks, with some products reaching 22C on delivery despite a recommended storage temperature of 8C. A microbiology professor warned that warm delivery conditions can allow bacteria to develop and make people ill.

The group also raised concerns about shipping, hygiene and missing Danish food labels, including information important to people with allergies. After Tænk contacted Temu, the platform removed most of its chilled foods from the Danish market. Temu said it was investigating concerns about cold storage and delivery; Tænk plans complaints to the relevant authorities.

perspectives.body: The test was limited to seven orders, but the consumer group says every product arrived at an excessive temperature. Temu has not explained why it removed the products.

content.headline: UK offers Denmark deeper military cooperation as it pitches frigates
content.shortHeadline: Britain links closer military ties with Denmark to frigate offer
content.standfirst: The UK is proposing joint operations and intelligence-sharing amid concern over Russian activity in the North Atlantic. A Danish decision on frigate purchases could influence how far the partnership develops, an analyst says.

image.caption: Britain’s aircraft carrier is central to its offer of deeper defence cooperation with Denmark.

sources.originalTitle: Storbritannien tilbyder militært samarbejde med Danmark – men det kommer med en pris

segments.body: Britain has offered Denmark a strategic defence partnership that could include joint operations, shared equipment and intelligence, with particular focus on the waters between Greenland, Iceland and the UK. The proposal comes amid reported increases in Russian military activity in the North Atlantic and Arctic.

The British offer also puts frigates at the centre of the proposed partnership. Denmark is considering offers from several countries and has not yet publicly responded. A Danish military analyst said Britain has a genuine interest in closer cooperation but suggested that enthusiasm could fall if Denmark buys frigates elsewhere. The Danish Defence Ministry confirmed dialogue with the UK but declined to comment further.

perspectives.body: The reporting distinguishes the security case for closer cooperation from Britain’s commercial interest in selling warships. The analyst said the two motives overlap, but the partnership could be less attractive to the UK if Denmark chooses another supplier.

content.headline: Low wind and little sunshine push Danish electricity prices to highest in years
content.shortHeadline: Danish power prices hit highest weekly average since 2022
content.standfirst: A period of low wind and solar output drove the highest weekly electricity prices since December 2022, according to Norlys. The company says gas power had to make up more of the shortfall as renewable generation fell across Europe.

image.caption: Low wind and solar generation during a dark, still period pushed up electricity prices.

source.credit: Foto: Ida Marie Odgaard / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Dunkelflaute giver de højeste elpriser i årevis

segments.body: The average wholesale electricity price last week reached 1.8 kroner per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 2 kroner in the east, the highest weekly averages since December 2022, according to energy company Norlys. A period of low wind and solar generation—known as “dunkelflaute”—reduced the supply of cheaper renewable electricity.

Norlys said gas power stations had to supply more electricity as wind and solar output fell across much of Europe, while the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have contributed to pressure on gas prices. The figures are for the wholesale price before tariffs, subscriptions and other charges; Norlys advised customers to shift flexible electricity use to cheaper hours.

perspectives.body: The price rise shows how weather across Europe can affect Danish power costs when wind and solar generation are low at the same time. The weekly average remains below the 2022 peak cited by Norlys.

content.headline: Climate scientist urges Denmark to push for stronger action at COP31
content.shortHeadline: Michael Mann urges Denmark to press for stronger climate action
content.standfirst: As the UN climate summit opens in Turkey, scientist Michael E. Mann says countries that recognise the threat should prevent opponents of climate action from blocking progress. He warns that risks from ice-sheet loss and other climate feedbacks remain difficult to time precisely.

image.caption: Climate scientist Michael E. Mann speaks with DR in New York.

sources.originalTitle: Vi er på vej ud i et minefelt, siger amerikansk stjerneforsker: Og vi risikerer ’katastrofale konsekvenser’ for hvert skridt

segments.body: Climate scientist Michael E. Mann has urged countries including Denmark to use their influence at COP31 to press for ambitious global climate action. He says the world has enough scientific evidence to recognise the threat from human-caused warming, while the United States under President Donald Trump is among the countries resisting action.

Mann said current national pledges would put the world on a path to about 2.7C of warming, according to the UN Environment Programme. He highlighted uncertain but potentially severe risks, including the loss of polar ice sheets and disruption to the Atlantic overturning circulation. “The further you move into the minefield,” he said, the greater the risk of triggering a catastrophic consequence.

content.headline: H1N1 may spread earlier in the US, but Denmark expects no unusually severe flu
content.shortHeadline: H1N1 could reach younger people; SSI does not expect a harsher season
content.standfirst: The 2009 pandemic strain is circulating in the US earlier than usual, and younger people may be more susceptible because many have not encountered it before. Danish researchers say the season has not yet taken off and do not expect it to be as intense as last year.

sources.originalTitle: Virus fra 2009-pandemi er tilbage og kan især smitte unge

segments.body: H1N1, the influenza strain behind the 2009 pandemic, is circulating early in the United States. A mutation may contribute to the timing, but US health authorities caution that an early rise does not necessarily mean a higher peak or more severe season. Denmark’s Statens Serum Institut says H1N1 is also expected to circulate here.

Some younger people may be more susceptible because they were not alive during the 2009 outbreak, although Danish researcher Ramona Trebbien said younger age generally reduces the risk of serious illness. SSI researcher Hanne-Dorthe Emborg said Denmark’s season had not yet begun in earnest and was not expected to be as intense as last year. The institute continues to recommend vaccination for older and vulnerable people.

perspectives.body: SSI clarified that describing an expected “high level” of flu does not mean a season will be worse than usual: the institute uses that term for a standard category in its respiratory-infection monitoring.

content.headline: Danish influencer awards criticised after no women win any prizes
content.shortHeadline: No women win at Danish creator awards, prompting criticism
content.standfirst: All 13 Simba Prisen awards went to men, prompting women creators to question representation. Winners of the regular categories are chosen by audience vote; organisers say they understand the criticism and will include it in their evaluation.

image.caption: The Simba Prisen awards show, where no women received a prize this year.

sources.originalTitle: 'En pølsefest': Mænd løb med samtlige priser til awardshow
'Simba Prisen' møder kritik efter prisuddeling uden kvindelige vindere

segments.body: No women won any of the 13 awards at Saturday’s Simba Prisen, which recognises Danish social-media creators. Several female influencers said the result left them feeling overlooked and raised questions for young women hoping to work in the field.

About 45,000 people voted, and organisers say the regular awards are decided by the audience. Some creators also questioned the categories and the absence of women among the winners, including the honorary award. Simba Prisen director Mia Marslew said the organisers understood the reaction and would take the criticism into their evaluation of future awards.

perspectives.body: TV 2 reports that at least one creator challenged the idea that audience voting absolves organisers of responsibility, arguing that category choices shape who can be represented on stage.

content.headline: Man Utd rescue 4-4 draw with Villa but remain in relegation zone
content.shortHeadline: United's stoppage-time fightback leaves Carrick under scrutiny
content.standfirst: Manchester United scored twice in stoppage time to salvage a point after trailing Aston Villa 4-2. The draw leaves them 18th, with Michael Carrick’s future still unclear.

image.caption: Manchester United draw 4-4 with Aston Villa after scoring twice in stoppage time.

sources.originalTitle: Bizarre & thrilling theatre as Carrick in limbo with Man Utd in drop zone

segments.body: United twice came back from two goals down in an eight-goal thriller at Old Trafford, with Patrick Dorgu equalising in the 96th minute. The point did little to ease their predicament: they remain 18th, in the relegation zone after at least 10 matches for the first time in 40 years.

segments.title: A reprieve, not a resolution
segments.body: United have not won a league match since 30 August and have conceded 15 goals in their past five. Carrick said he would not walk away, but did not confirm what discussions with the club’s hierarchy would follow. Defender Diogo Dalot was jeered as he left the field, amid wider fan anger.

content.headline: England thrash Australia 45-22 to ease pressure on Borthwick
content.shortHeadline: Seven-try England answer questions over Borthwick
content.standfirst: England scored seven tries in their most complete display of the year, giving coach Steve Borthwick a timely lift after questions over the team’s form and unity. Injuries to Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Seb Atkinson remain a concern.

image.caption: England beat Australia 45-22 to ease pressure on Steve Borthwick.

sources.originalTitle: England swat aside Wallabies to back up Borthwick
Feyi-Waboso burns bright as England energy endorses Borthwick

segments.body: England beat Australia 45-22 at Allianz Stadium, scoring seven tries in a performance that offered emphatic on-field backing for Borthwick. Henry Pollock scored twice, while Ben Spencer added a late try; Australia replied with three tries.

segments.title: A boost, with injury worries
segments.body: Feyi-Waboso left at half-time and later appeared in a protective boot, while centre Seb Atkinson also went off with a leg injury. England’s next steps will depend in part on the extent of those injuries.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport’s analysis highlighted the team’s visible energy and willingness to take attacking risks as part of the response to questions about unity—not just a display of physical force.

content.headline: Alcaraz beats Shelton to win his first Paris Masters title
content.shortHeadline: Alcaraz claims first Paris Masters crown against Shelton
content.standfirst: Carlos Alcaraz beat Ben Shelton in straight sets to claim the Paris Masters for the first time. It is his third title in the 17 matches since returning from a wrist injury.

image.caption: Carlos Alcaraz at the Paris Masters, where he won his first title at the tournament.

sources.originalTitle: Alcaraz takes revenge on Shelton to win first Paris Masters title

segments.body: Alcaraz defeated world number four Shelton 7-6 (7-5) 7-5 to win his first Paris Masters title. The Spaniard saved all six break points he faced in the opening set and recovered after Shelton threatened to take control in the second.

segments.title: A strong finish to the comeback
segments.body: The 23-year-old has won three titles and lost once in 17 matches since returning from a four-month wrist-injury absence. He goes into the ATP Finals on a nine-match winning streak after also winning in Vienna.

content.headline: Rahm holds off Hatton and McIlroy to win Abu Dhabi title
content.shortHeadline: Rahm wins Abu Dhabi as Hatton finishes two shots back
content.standfirst: Jon Rahm closed with a 67 to win the Abu Dhabi Championship by two shots from Tyrrell Hatton. Rory McIlroy finished third, four strokes behind the champion.

image.caption: Jon Rahm at the Abu Dhabi Championship, where he claimed his sixth Rolex Series title.

sources.originalTitle: Rahm pips Hatton & McIlroy to Abu Dhabi title

segments.body: Rahm finished at 23 under par after a final-round 67, with Hatton second on 21 under. McIlroy ended a further two shots back on 19 under. The Spaniard secured his sixth Rolex Series title and his first DP World Tour victory in four years.

segments.title: McIlroy’s season-long position
segments.body: McIlroy’s third place moved him to second in the Race to Dubai standings ahead of next week’s season finale. Rahm’s victory also keeps him in contention in that standings race.

content.headline: Leeds condemn racist abuse of Bogle after Tottenham win
content.shortHeadline: Leeds condemn online racist abuse of Jayden Bogle
content.standfirst: Leeds say they will work with authorities to identify those responsible for online racist abuse of Jayden Bogle. The messages followed a disputed tackle during the club’s 1-0 win over Tottenham.

image.caption: Leeds United defender Jayden Bogle.

sources.originalTitle: Leeds condemn racist abuse of Bogle after Tel incident

segments.body: Leeds condemned the racist abuse directed at defender Jayden Bogle after Saturday’s win over Tottenham, calling it “disgusting”. The abuse followed a first-half tackle on Mathys Tel for which referee John Brooks did not send Bogle off after a VAR review.

segments.title: Clubs call for action
segments.body: Leeds said it would work with the Premier League and relevant authorities to identify those responsible and seek the strongest possible action. Tottenham also condemned the abuse and offered support. The clubs’ statements stressed that online racism must not be excused by on-pitch disputes.

content.headline: Palace discuss Sage’s future after fourth straight league defeat
content.shortHeadline: Palace weigh Sage’s future after fourth league loss in a row
content.standfirst: Crystal Palace have held internal talks about manager Pierre Sage’s position after a 3-1 defeat by Liverpool left them bottom of the Premier League. No decision on his future has been confirmed.

image.caption: Crystal Palace’s defeat by Liverpool has increased pressure on manager Pierre Sage.

sources.originalTitle: Palace consider replacing Sage, with Frank among contenders

segments.body: Palace’s loss to Liverpool was their fourth successive league defeat and left them with seven points from 10 matches. The club have held talks about Sage’s future and possible replacements; former Tottenham and Brentford manager Thomas Frank is viewed as a strong candidate, with Sean Dyche also supported by some internally.

segments.title: Sage says work must improve
segments.body: Sage said the results were not good enough and that he needed to improve the team’s way of playing. Palace have conceded 24 league goals, the most in the division, but the report also notes injuries and player absences that have complicated his plans.

content.headline: Chengdu surrender 12-point lead as Dalian win Chinese title
content.shortHeadline: Chengdu collapse as Dalian take Chinese league title
content.standfirst: Chengdu lost their final four matches and missed out on the Chinese Super League title, despite once holding a 12-point lead. Dalian finished level on points but won on head-to-head record.

sources.originalTitle: Chengdu lose four in a row to blow 12-point lead & miss out on Chinese title

segments.body: Chengdu lost 3-2 to Shandong Taishan on the final day, while Dalian beat Tianjin 3-1 to claim the title. Both finished on 52 points, but Dalian took the championship on head-to-head record after also beating Chengdu in the penultimate game.

segments.title: A late-season reversal
segments.body: Chengdu had led by 12 points but picked up just one point from their final five matches. Dalian took all 15 available points over that stretch to complete a remarkable turnaround.

content.headline: Guehi scan leaves England availability uncertain
content.shortHeadline: Guehi faces scan as England wait on hip injury
content.standfirst: Marc Guehi will be assessed after asking to come off at half-time of Manchester City’s defeat by Nottingham Forest. England have yet to determine whether the defender can join the squad.

image.caption: Manchester City defender Marc Guehi.

sources.originalTitle: England await Guehi scan results after injury concern

segments.body: The Manchester City defender is due to have a scan on a hip complaint after leaving Saturday’s defeat at half-time. Manager Enzo Maresca said Guehi had asked to be substituted, and the issue is understood to have troubled him in recent weeks.

segments.title: England decision still pending
segments.body: Guehi has been a regular for Thomas Tuchel’s England side, but his availability for the upcoming international matches against Croatia and Spain is uncertain. England medical staff may also want to assess him before a final decision is made.

content.headline: Eurovision Song Contest Asia begins in Bangkok with 11 countries competing
content.shortHeadline: Eurovision Asia launches in Bangkok with 11 countries competing
content.standfirst: The contest’s first Asian edition brings acts from 11 countries to Bangkok on 14 November. Organisers hope to build a regional event, but questions remain over its audience, voting and how Eurovision’s traditions will travel.

image.caption: Eurovision Song Contest Asia entrants from Bhutan, South Korea and the Philippines.

sources.originalTitle: Eurovision is heading to Asia: here’s what to expect
Eurovision’s Asia experiment gets under way in flamboyant Bangkok

segments.body: The first Eurovision Song Contest Asia final is scheduled for Bangkok on 14 November, with 11 countries competing: Bhutan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. Organisers say they intend this to be the first of several regional editions. The show will be streamed on Eurovision’s YouTube channel and broadcast in each participating country.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s on-the-ground report finds signs of limited early interest: a week before the final, tickets remained available and the contest’s Asian social-media account had about 65,000 followers. Eurovision scholar Dean Vuletic also warns that the format’s European origins may make it harder to establish elsewhere.

segments.title: A new regional format, familiar questions
segments.body: The format follows the European contest: countries send one act, and a mix of national juries and public votes decides the winner. Viewers elsewhere can vote too, but those votes are pooled into a 12th territory. The winner will not automatically host the following year; organisers say that could be difficult for smaller countries.

segments.title: Traditions may not travel unchanged
segments.body: Organisers say it is too early to know whether bloc voting will emerge. The reporting notes possible regional ties, as well as tensions between Thailand and Cambodia, whose border dispute remains unresolved. Whether the contest’s camp style and queer culture will translate is also uncertain: one expert cautions that participating countries have different laws and media environments.

content.headline: Macklemore says nine US arenas rejected his Palestine benefit tour
content.shortHeadline: Macklemore says nine US arenas rejected his Palestine benefit tour
content.standfirst: The rapper says venues withdrew available dates after learning his planned shows would raise funds for Palestine. His account follows his removal from Ed Sheeran’s US tour; the named arenas have not responded in this reporting.

image.caption: Macklemore performs on the Free Palestine tour in Dublin.

sources.originalTitle: Macklemore says that nine US arenas turned down his Free Palestine tour

segments.body: Macklemore says nine major US arenas turned down his proposed Free Palestine benefit tour, including Madison Square Garden, Barclays Center and Crypto.com Arena. In an Instagram post, he alleges that dates initially offered for later this year were taken off the table after venues learned the shows were fundraisers for Palestine. The report includes no response from the arenas.

segments.title: A dispute over the US tour
segments.body: The claims follow Macklemore’s removal from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after the rapper made a speech supporting Palestine. Sheeran said venues had told him they would refuse to host the tour if Macklemore remained as a supporting act. Sheeran also said that choosing not to speak publicly about the conflict did not mean he lacked personal views or concern.

segments.title: Macklemore vows to keep organising
segments.body: Macklemore describes the venue decisions as intimidation and suppression of his political speech, and says he plans to continue organising benefit shows. He points to sold-out European dates in Dublin, Paris and London as evidence of support. The reporting presents his allegations and statements, but does not independently establish why the venues declined.

content.headline: Spice Girls’ 30th-anniversary Singles Collection offers more packaging than new
content.shortHeadline: Spice Girls’ anniversary box set offers little new for fans
content.standfirst: The band’s 30th-anniversary release packages 160 tracks across CDs or vinyl, but most have appeared in earlier reissues. The review finds the collection’s main novelty in a previously unreleased song featuring Victoria Beckham on lead vocals.

image.caption: The Spice Girls during their 1990s heyday.

sources.originalTitle: Spice Girls: The Singles Collection review – stop fleecing your fans right now, thank you very much

segments.body: After social-media teasers raised hopes of a reunion, the Spice Girls announced a box set rather than a tour or documentary. The Singles Collection gathers their singles, B-sides, remixes and demos in a 14-CD set, with a 7-inch vinyl version also available. Its price and the amount of previously repackaged material prompt the review’s central complaint: fans are being asked to pay for an anniversary product with little new music.

segments.title: One archival curiosity stands out
segments.body: The notable unreleased track is “Do You Think About Me,” recorded when the group was still called Touch. Its particular interest, the reviewer says, is Victoria Beckham’s lead vocal: she sounds confident on a song that moves between sweetness and a more forceful delivery. The compilation also collects enjoyable early B-sides, even as the large number of remixes makes the set feel overwhelming.

segments.title: The songs still make the case
segments.body: The critique is of the packaging, not the group’s catalogue. The review highlights the lasting energy of “Wannabe,” “Say You’ll Be There” and “Stop,” along with the band’s ballads. But repeated anniversary releases and merchandise, it argues, risk burying the music beneath another round of products for fans.

content.headline: Wynonna Judd’s new album turns family grief and hardship into song
content.shortHeadline: Wynonna Judd turns grief and hardship into a raw new album
content.standfirst: After a decade without an album, the country singer returns with The Hard Truth, a pared-back record shaped by family loss and personal struggle. She describes making it as part of her healing, with songs that address her mother and daughter directly.

image.caption: Wynonna Judd, whose new album is The Hard Truth.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I went into a deep, deep hole’: Wynonna Judd on overcoming family tragedy and putting a lifetime of love and pain into her new album

segments.body: The Hard Truth is Wynonna Judd’s first album in a decade. She has left behind the polished Nashville sound of earlier work for a rawer blend of country, blues and soul, co-writing nearly every track. Judd says she made the record as an act of healing after years of personal upheaval: “There’s a lot of love and pain on this record,” she says. “It’s very raw and very real.”

segments.title: Songs facing family loss
segments.body: The album addresses Judd’s mother Naomi, who died by suicide in 2022, the day before the Judds were due to be inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame. On “All Downhill from Ashland,” Wynonna sings directly to her mother about the cost of their shared musical life. Another song, “Girl Who Could Sing,” addresses the biological father she learned about as an adult and never had the chance to meet.

segments.title: A difficult present, too
segments.body: Judd also speaks about her adult daughter’s addiction and says she is raising her four-year-old granddaughter. She calls the child a blessing and a reason to face each morning. The interview places these ongoing pressures alongside Judd’s return to music, rather than presenting the album as a neat resolution to grief.

content.headline: Rita Wilson’s new album charts a woman’s life and a late-blooming voice
content.shortHeadline: Rita Wilson finds her voice on a new album about womanhood
content.standfirst: On Sound of a Woman, the actor and songwriter explores ageing, motherhood, illness and self-acceptance. Wilson also reflects on Hollywood’s ageism and why songwriting gave her room to say things her acting roles did not.

image.caption: Rita Wilson, whose album Sound of a Woman is out now.

sources.originalTitle: Rita Wilson: ‘My body turned on me – but it was also there to heal me’

segments.body: Rita Wilson says Sound of a Woman grew from a desire to explore women’s lives, from young love to loss and ageing. Across country-flavoured songs, she writes about body image, motherhood and finding a voice later in life. She began pursuing songwriting in her fifties, after feeling that the acting roles offered to her had become repetitive.

segments.title: Speaking beyond the roles
segments.body: Wilson says Hollywood remains “a very youth-oriented business” and that she once felt nervous about saying so publicly. Songwriting, she explains, gave her a way to express ideas she had not been asked to explore in her acting work. She points to “Spare Keys” as a song about breaking with an old self and allowing a new one to emerge.

segments.title: A song about the body
segments.body: The album also includes “Whose Body Is This?”, which Wilson connects to the changes her body has undergone, including a bilateral mastectomy after breast cancer. She describes the song as an attempt at acceptance and gratitude: her body, she says, was also there to help her heal.

content.headline: Richard Thompson looks back on Fairport Convention’s tragedy and a life in folk
content.shortHeadline: Richard Thompson reflects on Fairport, loss and his new album
content.standfirst: The folk guitarist discusses his 20th solo album, his London musical roots and the 1969 van crash that killed Fairport Convention drummer Martin Lamble and designer Jeannie Franklyn. He says the band did not know how to process the loss.

image.caption: Richard Thompson, the folk guitarist and former Fairport Convention member.

sources.originalTitle: Fairport Convention’s Richard Thompson on the crash that killed his bandmate

segments.body: Richard Thompson has released Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the latest in a six-decade career that began with Fairport Convention. He says he remains committed to making music that does not sound “overly American,” even though he has lived in the US for much of the past 35 years. His new songs draw on a cast of characters and memories from his past.

segments.title: A loss the band still remembers
segments.body: In 1969, a road accident on the way back from a Birmingham gig killed Fairport drummer Martin Lamble, 19, and Jeannie Franklyn, Thompson’s girlfriend. Thompson, who was in the van, recalls trying to reach Franklyn after the crash. “We did not deal with it,” he says, describing a time when the band had no support mechanism and quickly returned to work.

segments.title: Memory as material
segments.body: Thompson says writing his memoir, Beeswing, prompted him to revisit experiences he had put aside. Some new songs draw on people and places from his life, while others take a more fictional route. He says he is still learning as a musician and is already considering another album and a musical.

content.headline: A Taylor Swift fan remembers discovering her on MySpace in 2006
content.shortHeadline: Before Taylor Swift was famous, a fan found her on MySpace
content.standfirst: Twenty years after Swift’s debut, a former teenage fan recalls the online community that formed around her early songs. The memory traces how direct contact and a sense of shared discovery helped make an unknown country singer feel like a friend.

image.caption: Taylor Swift as a teenage country singer early in her career.

sources.originalTitle: The Taylor Swift I knew on MySpace in 2006

segments.body: The writer first found Taylor Swift through MySpace, after a friend sent a link to the page of a teenage country singer inspired by the Dixie Chicks. In 2006, before Swift’s rise to global stardom, the writer and other young fans traded comments, collected press clippings and waited for the debut album.

segments.title: A sense of being part of it
segments.body: Swift’s blogs, fan interactions and stories about school and life on the road made her seem familiar to the writer and friends. Their enthusiasm became a shared project: they recruited other fans online and treated each radio play or new press mention as a collective milestone. The essay recalls that connection without overlooking the promotional strategy and family support around Swift’s early career.

segments.title: Hearing the songs again
segments.body: The self-titled debut, released in October 2006, turned teenage heartbreak into direct, melodic songs that the writer remembers sharing on profile pages and message statuses. With hindsight, the essay considers how an artist who made young fans feel like outsiders would become one of the world’s biggest musicians, changing expectations of what women songwriters could control in their careers.

content.headline: Bob Dylan’s 1976 Rolling Thunder recordings bring a lost tour into focus
content.shortHeadline: Bob Dylan’s Rolling Thunder Revue gets its 1976 story back
content.standfirst: A 39-disc archive and two full concerts illuminate the spring 1976 leg of Dylan’s Rolling Thunder Revue, long overshadowed by its 1975 predecessor. The review finds a volatile, searching performer in recordings that complicate the tour’s familiar legend.

sources.originalTitle: The Rolling Thunder Revue: The 1976 Live Recordings

segments.body: A new archive gathers professionally recorded material from Bob Dylan’s 1976 Rolling Thunder Revue, including full versions of the Fort Worth and Fort Collins concerts. The release also comes in smaller standalone sets. The review argues that it corrects the impression that the tour’s second run was merely an afterthought to the better-known 1975 shows.

segments.title: An unsettled Dylan on stage
segments.body: The performances reveal a singer the reviewer describes as funny, mean, ragged and sharply focused. Dylan and the band rework songs including “Tangled Up in Blue,” “Shelter from the Storm” and “Idiot Wind,” giving them a more confrontational edge. The full concerts, the review says, make it possible to hear the flow and context that the old live album Hard Rain left out.

segments.title: A different kind of ending
segments.body: The tour’s 1976 close replaces the communal “This Land Is Your Land” ending of the previous year with “Gotta Travel On,” before a rare encore of “A Hard Rain’s A-Gonna Fall.” The review reads that change against a more uncertain political moment and sees the concert recordings as a forceful close to one phase of Dylan’s career.

content.headline: Michelle Yeoh on becoming a replicant and refusing Hollywood stereotypes
content.shortHeadline: Michelle Yeoh on Blade Runner, reinvention and refusing stereotypes
content.standfirst: The actor discusses playing a replicant in Blade Runner 2099 and the career turns that took her from ballet to Hong Kong action films and Hollywood. She also reflects on the limited roles offered to Asian actors and the films that helped shift expectations.

image.caption: Michelle Yeoh, who plays Olwen in Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Life is like a heartbeat. It’s up and down, up and down’: Michelle Yeoh on casting cliches, marriage at 60 and playing a robot in Blade Runner 2099

segments.body: In Blade Runner 2099, Michelle Yeoh plays Olwen, a replicant facing a programmed end. Yeoh says she wanted the character to feel fluid rather than conventionally robotic, and built her performance around questions of what it means to be human. The series is set decades after Blade Runner 2049, in a world where replicants have power and humans occupy a subordinate position.

segments.title: A career of pivots
segments.body: Yeoh trained in ballet before a back injury forced her to reconsider that ambition. A beauty pageant led to acting work in Hong Kong, where she became known for martial-arts films. She says Hollywood later offered her stereotyped Asian roles, which she declined, before Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon and Crazy Rich Asians helped open different possibilities.

segments.title: Movement, stillness and change
segments.body: Yeoh describes herself as an actor who likes to work out a character’s physical life. She contrasts the movement of her action roles with the stillness that can make a small expression carry weight. Her account ranges from her Oscar-winning work in Everything Everywhere All at Once to the personal decisions and career reversals that shaped her path.

content.headline: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52
content.shortHeadline: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman, dies aged 52
content.standfirst: The Chilean filmmaker’s death was announced by his partner, Amalia Kassai; no cause was given. Lelio’s films moved between intimate stories and political questions, including the Oscar-winning A Fantastic Woman and the internationally acclaimed Gloria.

image.caption: A still from Sebastián Lelio’s A Fantastic Woman.

sources.originalTitle: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52
Sebastián Lelio was a fascinating film-maker of great passion and poetry

segments.body: Sebastián Lelio has died aged 52, according to an announcement by his partner, Amalia Kassai. She did not give a cause of death. Chilean media reported that he died at his home in Santiago. Born in Argentina, Lelio moved to Chile as a child and went on to make films in Spanish and English.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s critic places Lelio among Chile’s leading filmmakers, emphasising his ability to make stories about ordinary lives feel both sensual and political. The essay identifies A Fantastic Woman as his most accomplished work.

segments.title: Stories of desire, grief and belonging
segments.body: Lelio’s films included Gloria, about a divorced woman searching for love and meaning; Disobedience, a story of queer desire within a conservative Jewish community; and The Wonder, adapted from Emma Donoghue’s novel. His final film, the musical protest drama The Wave, premiered at Cannes in 2025.

segments.title: The impact of A Fantastic Woman
segments.body: A Fantastic Woman follows Marina, a transgender woman denied the chance to grieve after the death of her partner. It won the Oscar for best international feature, becoming the first Chilean film to do so. Lelio said its release helped revive discussion of gender identity legislation in Chile.

content.headline: Wicker’s bizarre romance invites debate about desire and devotion
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s strange romance asks what women want from men
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a fantasy about a husband woven from willow. The film’s deliberately skewed relationship has prompted both comic fascination and criticism over whose desires matter.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it
A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who commissions a basketmaker to make her a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård. The result is a bawdy village fantasy in which the new husband eagerly tends to his wife’s needs. The i Paper’s reviewer calls the film funny and audacious, but also questions its portrayal of a partner with little apparent agency.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s reporting on the film’s reception connects the wicker husband’s appeal to current conversations about domestic labour and the mental load in relationships. Its filmmakers say they wanted a partner who helps without expecting praise.

segments.title: The fantasy behind the jokes
segments.body: The review argues that the husband’s unquestioning devotion raises an uneasy question: can a relationship be love if one partner has no meaningful freedom? It also sees the film as a fairy tale rather than a realistic model, and finds a more serious thread in the frustration of women living under the village’s unequal expectations.

segments.title: Why the unusual lead caught on
segments.body: The BBC report describes the online response to the trailer and the film’s deliberately strange romantic premise. Writers and researchers interviewed there place Wicker within a wider tradition of human-monster romances, where outsiders and unconventional desire can challenge assumptions about beauty, power and partnership.

content.headline: Fifty years after Rocky, the underdog story still has a fresh punch
content.shortHeadline: Rocky at 50: the underdog story and how Stallone made it
content.standfirst: A cinema reissue revisits Sylvester Stallone’s 1976 boxing drama as a new film, I Play Rocky, recounts the fight to get it made. Together, the review and reporting trace the film’s blend of working-class struggle and stubborn idealism.

image.caption: Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa in the 1976 film.

sources.originalTitle: Rocky review – 50 years on, Stallone’s boxer remains an exhilaratingly gritty contender
'It was a total miracle': How rejection led Sylvester Stallone to create film's ultimate underdog Rocky

segments.body: Rocky began with Sylvester Stallone, then an unknown actor struggling to find substantial roles, writing a part for himself. He refused offers to sell the screenplay unless he could play Rocky Balboa. The new film I Play Rocky dramatises that insistence and the low-budget production that followed; the original Rocky returns to cinemas for its 50th anniversary.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s review sees the original as a departure from the fatalism of earlier boxing films: Rocky loses the fight but wins a moral victory, turning a familiar tale of struggle into a rousing story of endurance.

segments.title: A gamble that paid off
segments.body: I Play Rocky’s account describes Stallone as broke and determined, even as the studio wanted an established star in the lead. Rocky was shot in 28 days on a budget of about $1m. It went on to become the biggest box-office hit of 1976, earn 10 Oscar nominations and win best picture.

segments.title: Why the story endures
segments.body: The original film follows a Philadelphia boxer offered an unlikely chance to fight heavyweight champion Apollo Creed. The review highlights its local texture and its idealistic refusal to deliver the expected betrayals. The feature on I Play Rocky argues that Stallone’s own outsider status is inseparable from the character’s appeal.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning turns Facebook’s failures into a warning about our feeds
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook’s power back on screen
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network revisits reporting on Facebook’s algorithms and their effects on users. The i Paper’s review finds a chilling film whose portrait of the platform’s power is sharpened by the reviewer’s own difficulty in leaving it.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: The Social Reckoning dramatises the reporting behind the Facebook Files, the 2021 investigation into the company’s internal research and its approach to content. The film follows reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by Jeremy Allen White, and whistleblower Frances Haugen, played by Mikey Madison, as they pursue concerns about the platform’s effects on teen mental health and political misinformation.

segments.title: A story that reaches into daily life
segments.body: The reviewer describes the film as both investigative drama and personal horror: its account of recommendation systems and outrage-driven engagement is difficult to separate from the viewer’s own use of social media. The essay’s central tension is that people may understand the harms and still feel that work, leisure and friendships depend on the same platforms.

segments.title: The reporting has moved on
segments.body: The film focuses on events that became public years ago. The review notes further controversies and the growth of Meta since the Facebook Files, while arguing that the repeated revelations have not necessarily prompted people to stop using its products. The film’s ending offers a measure of hope, but does not resolve that contradiction.

content.headline: Renate Reinsve on the role that nearly came after she quit acting
content.shortHeadline: Renate Reinsve on the film that brought her back to acting
content.standfirst: The Norwegian actor thought The Worst Person in the World might be her last film before Joachim Trier wrote a leading role for her. Reinsve reflects on the collaboration, her later work in Fjord and why she values films that leave room for audiences to decide what to feel.

sources.originalTitle: 'It stopped me quitting acting': Renate Reinsve on her life-changing role in The Worst Person in the World

segments.body: Renate Reinsve was planning to leave acting when Joachim Trier offered her the leading role in The Worst Person in the World. She says the film changed her life. Its Cannes success and her best-actress prize brought new opportunities after years in which she struggled to find screen roles she wanted.

segments.title: A character that felt familiar
segments.body: Reinsve describes Julie, the restless central character, as someone she recognised. The film follows Julie as she changes jobs and relationships while approaching 30, without presenting her choices as a simple path to certainty. Reinsve says the work felt honest because people on set found parts of themselves in the character’s contradictions.

segments.title: A different challenge in Fjord
segments.body: Reinsve’s role in Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord is markedly different: she plays Lisbet, a quiet mother whose children are taken into care after allegations of abuse. Reinsve says she wanted to understand the character without judging her. She also values the film’s refusal to tell viewers exactly what to think.

content.headline: Fourteen box-office flops that found an audience after release
content.shortHeadline: 14 film flops that deserve another look
content.standfirst: From The Thing and Dune to Babylon and Furiosa, this guide revisits films that failed commercially or were dismissed on release. Its case is that box-office disappointment does not settle a film’s value.

image.caption: A selection of films once regarded as box-office failures.

sources.originalTitle: The 14 spectacular film flops that are actually worth watching

segments.body: The list argues that commercial failure can obscure films worth revisiting. It ranges across genres and decades, pairing familiar misfires with later reassessments: John Carpenter’s The Thing, David Lynch’s Dune, the Coen brothers’ The Hudsucker Proxy and George Miller’s Furiosa are among the selections.

segments.title: A different reception over time
segments.body: Some entries were out of step with the moment: The Thing opened in the shadow of E.T., while Last Action Hero arrived just after Jurassic Park. Others, including Dredd and Cloud Atlas, are presented as ambitious films that struggled to find a broad audience despite their distinctive ideas.

segments.title: A recommendation, not a verdict
segments.body: The guide also includes films whose reputations have shifted, such as Heaven’s Gate and Babylon. Its argument is not that every disappointment is secretly a masterpiece, but that opening-weekend performance and later cultural life are different measures—and that a second look may reveal pleasures the first reception missed.

content.headline: The Good Daughter review: Rose Byrne leads a glossy thriller packed with trauma
content.shortHeadline: The Good Daughter: Rose Byrne leads a glossy, twisty thriller
content.standfirst: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy play estranged sisters drawn back into a violent family history. The Guardian finds the opening almost comically relentless, but says the series settles into a more engaging drama when it focuses on the sisters together.

image.caption: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy as sisters Samantha and Charlotte in The Good Daughter.

sources.originalTitle: The Good Daughter: Rose Byrne’s legal thriller is so full of calamity it borders on Mr Bean-like farce

segments.body: The Good Daughter begins with a traumatic childhood event and quickly adds more violence, setting up a story about sisters Samantha and Charlotte Quinn. Byrne plays Samantha, a successful New York lawyer; Fahy plays Charlotte, who stayed in their Georgia hometown and became a lawyer like their father. A new crisis brings the sisters back together.

segments.title: The sisters are the strongest draw
segments.body: The review says the opening piles on so many shocks that it risks tipping into farce. The drama becomes more effective when it slows down and lets the sisters interact, including in a scene where they scramble to shut a coffin lid. Fahy, the reviewer says, holds her own opposite Byrne and gives their relationship warmth as well as tension.

segments.title: A familiar, polished thriller
segments.body: Adapted by Karin Slaughter from her novel, the series links a new murder to the family’s earlier trauma and the wider community. The review finds its plotting familiar and its presentation too polished, but suggests its broad appeal may make it a major audience draw for Byrne.

content.headline: The Assassin season two review: Keeley Hawes’s spy thriller loses its way
content.shortHeadline: The Assassin’s second season is sunk by its son’s whining
content.standfirst: Keeley Hawes returns as a midlife assassin, but the Guardian argues that her character’s relationship with her anxious adult son overwhelms the show. The review finds the thriller’s central pairing more damaging than its already convoluted plotting.

image.caption: Keeley Hawes and Freddie Highmore in The Assassin.

sources.originalTitle: The Assassin review – will anybody save Keeley Hawes from this unbearably pathetic boy?

segments.body: Season two opens with Julie Green, played by Keeley Hawes, still working as a hired killer. When her son Edward’s wife is kidnapped on honeymoon, he turns to Julie for help. The story resumes the series’ mix of family secrets, conspiracies and violent set pieces.

segments.title: A mismatch at the centre
segments.body: The review praises Hawes but finds Freddie Highmore’s Edward written as so timid and persistently alarmed that he drains the tension from the thriller. It also argues that Julie’s potential as a menopausal assassin is left largely unexplored, with her scenes too often reduced to sniping and sitcom-style bickering.

segments.title: More twists, less character
segments.body: The series continues to raise mysteries about kidnappings, past events and hidden motives, but the review regards that narrative sprawl as secondary to the central relationship. It concludes that the show’s attempt to build a long-running premise is undermined by characters who are difficult to spend time with.

content.headline: Black Doves season two review: a spy drama built on friendship and chaos
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves returns with implausible plots and winning chemistry
content.standfirst: Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw and Sarah Lancashire return to Joe Barton’s espionage series. The Guardian accepts its outlandish conspiracies as part of the fun, finding its strongest thread in the friendship between Helen and Sam.

image.caption: Ben Whishaw and Keira Knightley in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Black Doves review – Ben Whishaw, Keira Knightley and Sarah Lancashire are spine-tinglingly good

segments.body: In the second season, spy Helen Webb is newly installed in No 10 while her handler, Reed, has disappeared. Helen calls on her close friend Sam, a hitman, and a collection of other assassins to help find Reed as questions gather around Helen’s cover story and the prime minister’s household.

segments.title: The cast makes the case
segments.body: The review says the show’s appeal lies less in the conspiracies than in its actors and characters. Knightley plays Helen’s social performance with precision; Whishaw gives Sam a melancholy charm, while Lancashire brings menace to Reed. Their chemistry helps the series move among espionage, comedy and farce.

segments.title: A friendship amid the mayhem
segments.body: The review notes that the show’s body count and the characters’ repeated escapes make it hard to believe in the stakes. But it finds a more grounded emotional centre in Helen and Sam’s friendship: their shared humour and loyalty offer connection amid the violence and elaborate deception.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors finale: Bash’s last-minute call turns the game
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors finale turns on Bash’s late suspicion
content.standfirst: After a series the reviewer found flat, the final round brings a surprise victory for the Faithful. Bash’s suspicion of Kenny—and his ability to persuade Romesh Ranganathan—changes the outcome and gives the show a late burst of tension.

image.caption: The Celebrity Traitors cast at the Endgame Round Table.

sources.originalTitle: One player’s lack of ego saved Celebrity Traitors

segments.body: The finale begins with the Traitors eliminating Michael Sheen, whom the reviewer regarded as the Faithful’s strongest hope. James Blunt then picks up Sheen’s suspicions and correctly identifies Maya Jama, who is banished at the final Round Table. The remaining Faithful, however, continue to misread the game.

segments.title: A reversal at the endgame
