segments.body: Kenny appears close to winning when he chooses to end the game with several players still present. Bash realises that the decision suggests Kenny may be a Traitor and votes against him. After the vote ties with James Blunt, Bash persuades Romesh Ranganathan to change his mind; Kenny is banished and the Faithful win £83,000 for charity.

segments.title: The player who kept his head
segments.body: The reviewer credits Bash’s lack of ego for the reversal, contrasting him with players whose confidence or performance drew attention. Bash had made mistakes earlier, but the piece argues that his willingness to reconsider at the crucial moment rescued a finale—and a series—that had seemed headed for a predictable Traitor win.

content.headline: The Matthew Perry documentary review: intimate, but does it add anything?
content.shortHeadline: Matthew Perry’s Netflix documentary feels intrusive, the review argues
content.standfirst: Netflix’s three-part series revisits the Friends actor’s addiction and death, though Perry had already written about much of his experience. The i Paper’s review finds moving testimony alongside an intrusive focus on his family’s grief and little new scrutiny of the circumstances.

image.caption: Matthew Perry in a photograph accompanying the Netflix documentary review.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: The One About Matthew Perry follows the actor from his early career through Friends, addiction and his death at 54 in 2023. The documentary includes archive footage and accounts from people close to him. The review notes that Perry’s 2022 memoir had already described his addiction and its effects in candid detail.

segments.title: Moving testimony, limited new reporting
segments.body: Perry’s sister describes the loneliness and pressure that accompanied his addiction, and the documentary’s archive material keeps the actor present on screen. But the review argues that the series adds little to what he said himself and moves quickly through questions about the ketamine supply and the people involved in his final months.

segments.title: The cost of access
segments.body: The critic is most troubled by the camera’s lingering attention to relatives recalling the moment they learned Perry had died. The piece asks whether the series serves viewers or the actor’s memory by revisiting that grief, and argues that Perry’s own account and his performances remain more respectful ways to remember him.

content.headline: Why Doctor Who’s future looks uncertain after its latest hiatus
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ deal ends
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to tender, with no new Doctor announced. The i Paper examines the show’s history and the questions facing its next revival.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since Ncuti Gatwa’s final series as the Doctor in 2025, the BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special. The corporation is seeking another partner to help fund the programme, but the report says no one has yet stepped forward and no successor to Gatwa has been announced.

segments.title: A show built on change
segments.body: The feature traces Doctor Who from its 1963 debut through its 1989 cancellation and 2005 revival. Regeneration let the series change its lead and tone, while keeping its central idea of curiosity and kindness. Fans and television historians interviewed say that renewal has been essential to the programme’s appeal.

segments.title: What went wrong—and what could return
segments.body: The article reports disagreement over the more recent scripts, the show’s audience and the value of its Disney+ deal. Some interviewees argue the latest Doctors deserved stronger material; others emphasise that the programme has survived earlier pauses. The future remains unresolved, but fans interviewed want it back on screen rather than preserved only in the archive.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family into The Split’s legal-drama world
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up gives its legal drama a new British Asian family
content.standfirst: The six-part spin-off moves the family-law firm from London to Manchester and centres a predominantly British Asian cast. Its creators say the aim is to retain The Split’s family melodrama while depicting characters living ordinary, contemporary lives.

image.caption: Ritu Arya and Abi Morgan at the centre of The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, played by Ritu Arya, a barrister expected to take over her family’s Manchester law firm. Her plans shift after her mother’s death alters the succession, and a former romantic partner arrives as a new colleague. As in The Split, weekly divorce cases run alongside fractures within the family.

segments.title: Representation as everyday life
segments.body: The spin-off features a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to show a British Asian family living ordinary lives, rather than relying on the limited storylines often assigned to such characters. Arya says she researched the role by speaking with a family lawyer.

segments.title: A familiar formula with new voices
segments.body: Original-series creator Abi Morgan remains an executive producer and describes the show’s appeal as a mix of family ties, ambition and betrayal. She says the new writing team has been able to carry those themes forward while developing its own characters and stories outside London.

content.headline: 70 Up ends a landmark documentary series—and reopens its old questions
content.shortHeadline: 70 Up ends a landmark series with questions about its gaze
content.standfirst: After six decades, ITV’s Seven Up! project reaches its final chapter. The i Paper revisits the lives of its contributors and the criticisms of director Michael Apted’s framing, asking what a long-running documentary can reveal—and what it leaves out.

image.caption: Contributors to the Seven Up! documentary project when they were children.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A little pill of poison’: Why the cast of 70 Up came to resent it

segments.body: The documentary project began in 1964, following 14 children from different backgrounds and returning to them every seven years. Its final instalment, 70 Up, catches up with the surviving participants. Asif Kapadia took over directing after Michael Apted’s death in 2021.

segments.title: A portrait with blind spots
segments.body: The feature revisits participants’ objections to how the series portrayed them. Some left; others felt the programme narrowed their lives into a role or a few minutes of screen time. Jackie Basset challenged Apted’s questions about women, while John Brisby objected to being cast as the token upper-class participant.

segments.title: What a long view can—and cannot—show
segments.body: The series remains a rare record of people growing older across changing circumstances, but the article stresses that edited documentaries cannot contain a whole life. Producer Helen Houston says early childhood shapes people, while one participant reflects that there was always more to him than the programme could show.

content.headline: Titanium Court review: an 8-bit fairy game where anything can happen
content.shortHeadline: Titanium Court is a strange, surprising game worth getting lost in
content.standfirst: AP Thomson’s strategy game mixes pixel-art fairies, Shakespearean framing and optional songs about Pacific salmon. The Guardian’s critic argues that its unpredictability is not a gimmick but the point of the experience.

image.caption: A scene from the pixel-art game Titanium Court.

sources.originalTitle: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites

segments.body: Titanium Court begins as a strategy game in which players match tiles and lead small fairy armies. It soon veers into strange territory: after a boss fight, a player might be offered a musical performance instead. The game’s developer, AP Thomson, wrote and recorded the music, including songs that can replace fights.

segments.title: A deliberately disorienting world
segments.body: The game’s 8-bit look, vivid pink palette and fairy-court setting frame a story full of theatrical references and unexpected digressions. Thomson says fairies gave him freedom to mix ideas, and that he wanted to move beyond familiar Tolkien-style fantasy. The reviewer argues that discovering the game’s peculiar logic is central to its appeal.

segments.title: Uncertainty as the pleasure
segments.body: The critic recommends avoiding spoilers: even after many hours, it is difficult to know what the game might do next. Its odd songs, conversations and encounters can feel startlingly personal, though Thomson says some moments emerged from combinations he had not expected players to find. It is now available on consoles and smartphones as well as PC.

content.headline: Black Tides Draga’s Wake lets a longtime games fan voice its hero
content.shortHeadline: A lifelong gamer finally voices a video-game hero
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s Dominik Diamond describes voicing Draga, a sailor in a survival-horror game made by a small, distributed team. The process turns a career-long love of games into a family memory—and a new appreciation for voice acting.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist of Black Tides Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: Dominik Diamond was invited to voice the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake, a survival-horror game set aboard a decaying steamship after a heist goes wrong. He initially doubted that his voice suited Draga, a tough sailor infected by an ancient god, but says adjusting his performance helped it work.

segments.title: Making a game together
segments.body: Diamond describes a team spread across the world, developing the game in their spare time. The experience reminded him of bedroom programming culture and showed him the creative energy that can exist outside large publishers. The most awkward task, he says, was improvising fight noises in a garage in rural Nova Scotia.

segments.title: A family moment
segments.body: Diamond played clips for his children without telling them he was in the game. He says their reaction when they recognised their father as an action hero became one of his favourite moments as a parent. The work also made him newly attentive to the acting and direction behind video-game performances.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans mourning a lost RPG future
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans with an unfinished future
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s Lucy James reflects on EA’s reported closure of the studio and cancellation of its next Mass Effect game. Her account combines the news with a personal explanation of why BioWare’s choice-driven worlds mattered to players.

image.caption: A scene from Mass Effect 3, part of BioWare’s role-playing game series.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The writer reports that EA has closed BioWare, ending a studio’s 30-year run of role-playing games, and cancelled its forthcoming Mass Effect title. The article says more than 400 people are losing their jobs. The author, a former games-industry worker and longtime fan, describes the decision as a major loss for the genre.

segments.title: A galaxy shaped by player choices
segments.body: James recalls how the Mass Effect trilogy drew her in through its characters and the decisions that carried across games. Players shaped Commander Shepard’s identity and relationships, and faced consequences for the alliances they made. The article argues that this sense of agency is central to the series’ enduring hold on its audience.

segments.title: A studio’s legacy, an uncertain sequel
segments.body: The piece acknowledges that BioWare had not produced a major critical or commercial hit in more than a decade and notes EA’s financial pressures. But it says the cancelled game had the potential to renew a much-loved universe. The closure, the writer argues, leaves western role-playing games with a smaller creative landscape.

content.headline: Baxdrostat may offer lasting blood-pressure relief for some patients
content.shortHeadline: Baxdrostat may offer lasting relief for some blood-pressure patients
content.standfirst: A small follow-up analysis found that some patients’ blood pressure stayed lower after they stopped taking the drug. Researchers say larger studies are needed before it can be called a lasting cure.

sources.originalTitle: New drug that could permanently cure high blood pressure coming to UK by 2027

segments.body: A follow-up analysis of a larger baxdrostat trial found that 14 patients with substantial blood-pressure reductions continued to have lower readings after stopping the drug. Their treatment lasted six to 12 months; the reported follow-up extends to two years, with one patient followed for three years.

segments.title: A finding that needs testing
segments.body: The researchers think the drug may have killed aldosterone-producing cells in small adrenal tumours, which can cause high blood pressure. But the proposed mechanism and lasting benefit are not established: the analysis involved a small group, and a larger study is under way. Baxdrostat’s approval in the US is for difficult-to-control high blood pressure, not a proven permanent cure.

content.headline: Lightning may change as the climate warms, with consequences for fires
content.shortHeadline: How a warming climate could change lightning and fire risk
content.standfirst: Lightning helps shape ecosystems, but changing storm conditions could also increase dangerous ignitions. Research suggests possible shifts, especially at higher latitudes, though projections vary widely.

image.caption: Lightning flashes across a storm-darkened sky.

sources.originalTitle: Thunderstruck: what does the future hold for lightning?

segments.body: Lightning is not only a hazard: it contributes to the nitrogen cycle and helps shape fire-dependent ecosystems. But a warming climate may change where and how often it strikes. A review of studies, still under peer review, found projections ranging from an 11% decrease to a 44% increase in lightning per degree of warming, with an average projected increase of 7.5%.

segments.title: Fire and uncertainty
segments.body: Researchers see broad agreement that lightning will increase at high latitudes, but are less certain about tropical regions. Dry lightning can ignite remote fires that are difficult to reach; the article cites Australian records showing 50% more dry-lightning strikes in south-eastern forests in 2000–16 than in the previous two decades. Lightning alone does not determine fire severity: dryness, heat and wind also matter.

content.headline: Scientists link enjoyable conversations to a balance of focus and fresh ideas
content.shortHeadline: Study links better conversations to a balance of focus and novelty
content.standfirst: In analyses of conversations between strangers, friends and speed-dating pairs, exchanges with a particular pattern of shifting between topics were linked to greater enjoyment and connection.

image.caption: Two people talk during a conversation.

sources.originalTitle: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’

segments.body: Researchers analysed more than 1,000 conversations between strangers, as well as chats between friends and speed-dating pairs. People tended to report more enjoyment and connection when conversations showed what the researchers call “pink noise”: staying with a subject long enough to explore it, then bringing in fresh ideas rather than becoming stuck or jumping randomly between topics.

segments.title: A pattern, not a recipe
segments.body: The team used an AI system to score each turn for meaning, tone and context, then assessed how the conversation changed over time. Pink noise was associated with enjoyment and, in speed-dating chats, predicting which pairs met again. The study does not establish that a conversational technique causes better relationships; a conversation analyst also cautioned that judging exchanges mainly by enjoyment can miss the importance of difficult or emotionally significant conversations.

content.headline: Was Verica, the Iron Age ruler who drew Rome to Britain, a queen?
content.shortHeadline: Was Verica, the ruler linked to Rome’s invasion, a queen?
content.standfirst: An archaeologist argues that coin designs and inscriptions could point to a female ruler, but other specialists say the evidence is inconclusive and some details may support a male reading.

sources.originalTitle: Historians say King Verica persuaded Rome to invade Britain. But could Verica actually have been a queen?

segments.body: Archaeologist Miles Russell argues that Verica, an Iron Age ruler who fled to Rome before the invasion of Britain in AD43, may have been a woman. His case draws on the name’s ending, the word “Rex” on coins, images that he interprets as feminine and inscriptions that he says could mean “daughter of” rather than “son of”.

segments.title: A disputed interpretation
segments.body: Other specialists quoted in the report say the evidence does not settle Verica’s sex. Roger Tomlin notes that some male Latin names end in “a” and says Russell has not shown that “Rex” was used for women as well as men. Coin expert Daphne Nash Briggs points to coins bearing apparently male figures; Russell disputes those readings. The theory remains a proposal, not an established historical conclusion.

content.headline: US prosecutors drop charges against Harvard scientist Kseniia Petrova
content.shortHeadline: US drops charges against Harvard scientist Kseniia Petrova
content.standfirst: Federal prosecutors have dismissed the case against the Russian scientist, who spent four months in immigration detention after arriving with frog-embryo samples for research. The reasons given focus on the government’s priorities and resources.

image.caption: Kseniia Petrova leaves a federal courthouse in Boston.

sources.originalTitle: US prosecutors drop criminal charges against scientist detained over frog embryos

segments.body: US prosecutors have dropped all criminal charges against Kseniia Petrova, a Harvard Medical School scientist who was arrested after returning from France with frog-embryo samples intended for research. The charges included smuggling, concealing facts and making false statements. A federal judge granted prosecutors’ request to dismiss the case.

segments.title: A disputed prosecution
segments.body: Prosecutors said the costs of continuing the case outweighed the public interest in resolving it, while describing Petrova’s claims of vindictive and selective prosecution as meritless. Her lawyer criticised the decision to bring charges; the Department of Homeland Security had maintained that she lied to federal officers. The report says Petrova had spent four months in immigration detention and feared deportation to Russia.

content.headline: SpaceX’s Starlink Mobile aims to become a US carrier, but the buildout is costly
content.shortHeadline: Starlink Mobile’s US carrier ambitions face a costly buildout
content.standfirst: SpaceX plans to combine satellite-to-phone service with a terrestrial mobile network, including spectrum and cell sites. The head of T-Mobile’s parent company says the project could require at least $200bn.

sources.originalTitle: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
T-Mobile owner on Elon Musk launching a wireless carrier: ‘Welcome to the party’

segments.body: SpaceX says it wants Starlink Mobile to compete with major US carriers by combining direct-to-cell satellites with a ground-based network. The plans described include acquiring low-band spectrum and using Qualcomm technology at tens of thousands of 5G sites, with deployments expected from 2027. SpaceX has also reportedly discussed access to cell towers and a possible deal involving Boost Mobile.

segments.title: The cost of competing
segments.body: Deutsche Telekom chief executive Tim Höttges, whose company owns T-Mobile, said SpaceX’s ambitions should be taken seriously but estimated that spectrum and network construction could require at least $200bn. That is his assessment, not a confirmed project budget. SpaceX’s plans remain dependent on building or accessing the terrestrial infrastructure as well as expanding satellite service.

perspectives.body: Höttges argues that spectrum is only part of the expense: SpaceX would also need towers and antennas to compete with established mobile networks. He sees a potential new kind of communications service, but says it will not come cheaply.

content.headline: TikTok videos may funnel young viewers toward adult-content platforms, study say
content.shortHeadline: Study says TikTok videos can steer young users toward adult content
content.standfirst: Researchers from two campaigning organisations say creators use coded references in lifestyle videos to promote paid sexual content elsewhere. TikTok and OnlyFans say they have rules and safeguards against sexual content and underage access.

image.caption: A person uses a phone displaying TikTok.

sources.originalTitle: TikTok accused of helping to promote sex industry to girls

segments.body: A report by UK and Australian campaigning organisations says some popular OnlyFans performers use TikTok lifestyle posts to hint at explicit material sold elsewhere. Researchers cite coded terms, emojis and links between accounts, alongside videos presenting paid sexual content as a route to wealth. The material they studied was non-explicit; the report argues that it can still promote the adult-content industry to young audiences.

segments.title: Platforms’ responses
segments.body: The researchers call for restrictions on under-18s seeing not only pornography but also posts that promote or relate to the sex industry. TikTok says it prohibits sexual content and uses technology to enforce its rules, including safeguards intended to keep age-inappropriate material from teens. OnlyFans says its service is for adults and that it has onboarding checks to prevent minors from accessing it.

content.headline: Philadelphia professor’s protests challenge sidewalk delivery robots
content.shortHeadline: A professor is blocking delivery robots to protest their use on city
content.standfirst: Carolyn Marvin says delivery robots do not belong in public space and argues that residents should have a say. The protest has drawn supporters and criticism, and she is contesting a disorderly-conduct ticket.

image.caption: Carolyn Marvin blocks a delivery robot during a protest in Philadelphia.

sources.originalTitle: Standing in the way of slop bowls: the woman blocking food delivery robots

segments.body: Carolyn Marvin, a semi-retired University of Pennsylvania professor, has repeatedly stood in front of Uber Eats delivery robots in Philadelphia to protest their presence on sidewalks. Police issued her a disorderly-conduct ticket after one confrontation; she says she will challenge it and invokes her right to protest in public space.

segments.title: Who are sidewalks for?
segments.body: Marvin argues that the robots may take jobs and create hazards for people with mobility issues, and says residents should have a say in whether private machines use public streets. Reactions are mixed: some passers-by support her, while others worry about interrupting deliveries. Pennsylvania law treats delivery robots as pedestrians, and the operator Avride says making the machines seem approachable helps people feel comfortable around them.

content.headline: South-east Asia reins in data-centre boom as power and water constraints mount
content.shortHeadline: Power and water pressures slow south-east Asia’s data-centre rush
content.standfirst: Thailand paused projects and Indonesia halted one development as governments and communities weigh resource demands. The region remains a major growth hub, but new approvals are increasingly tied to energy and water requirements.

image.caption: A data centre stands within a residential area in Thailand.

sources.originalTitle: The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east Asia

segments.body: South-east Asia’s data-centre expansion is running into limits on power, water and planning. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and decisions on 117 more in September, while authorities in Indonesia’s West Java halted a development over permits and an incomplete environmental assessment. The region has a large share of Asia-Pacific capacity under construction, much of it in Malaysia and Thailand.

segments.title: Who bears the costs?
segments.body: Wood Mackenzie estimates that data centres already use 24% of the power consumed in Malaysia’s Johor state, a share that could reach 40% by 2035. Water needs are also a concern in drought-prone Johor and in parts of Thailand where reservoirs are under strain. Governments are tightening approval frameworks, while an academic quoted in the report questions whether communities receive benefits proportionate to the infrastructure and environmental costs.

content.headline: DataVita drops direct-renewables claim for Scottish AI data-centre plan
content.shortHeadline: Scottish AI data-centre plan now relies on the National Grid
content.standfirst: DataVita has revised its plan for a Lanarkshire project, saying the site will be grid-served and that wind and solar could connect later. The change raises questions about earlier claims of direct renewable supply.

image.caption: The existing DataVita data centre at Chapelhall, near Airdrie.

sources.originalTitle: Lanarkshire AI datacentre to fully rely on National Grid despite renewables claim

segments.body: DataVita now says its proposed data centres near Chapelhall, Lanarkshire, will be “fully grid served”, with wind and solar projects potentially connected in future. That differs from an earlier claim that more than 1GW of renewable capacity would be delivered through private connections to the site.

segments.title: The company’s explanation
segments.body: DataVita says its commitment to renewable energy is unchanged and that grid power would be covered by a renewable power-purchase agreement. The report notes that the company has public wealth guarantees and that its project has been promoted as part of the UK’s AI strategy. An environmental campaigner quoted by the Guardian describes the shift as emblematic of exaggerated claims by data-centre developers.

content.headline: Google takes over troubled Wyoming data-centre project from Crusoe
content.shortHeadline: Google takes over an unfinished Wyoming data-centre project
content.standfirst: Crusoe has sold an unfinished site to Google, which plans to invest $17bn in its development. The handover highlights the difficulty of securing power, equipment and schedules for very large AI infrastructure projects.

sources.originalTitle: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google

segments.body: Data-centre developer Crusoe has sold an unfinished project in south-eastern Wyoming to Google, which announced plans to invest $17bn in the campus. Crusoe had previously sought Google as a customer for the project. Google reportedly raised concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management; the purchase price was not disclosed.

segments.title: A difficult buildout
segments.body: The project was initially announced with a plan to scale to 10 gigawatts. The report says large data-centre developments depend on securing equipment and power and can also be complicated by local opposition. Crusoe continues to develop other facilities for major technology companies, so the Wyoming sale is a setback on one project rather than an end to its wider business.

content.headline: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as sales trail its early ambitions
content.shortHeadline: Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production after weak sales
content.standfirst: Elon Musk says production at Tesla’s Texas factory will be reduced next year to make room for Cybercabs. Sales have fallen well short of his earlier forecast, though the company has not said the vehicle will disappear entirely.

sources.originalTitle: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
Good riddance, Cybertruck!

segments.body: Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory next year to make room for more Cybercab production. He did not say whether the vehicle will be discontinued or made elsewhere. The project’s lead engineer appeared to suggest it was ending, while Musk said the existing fleet would remain on the road for a long time.

segments.title: Ambitions and sales
segments.body: Tesla sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in 2025, down from 38,965 the year before, according to figures cited by the BBC. Musk had forecast annual sales of 250,000. The Verge’s analysis argues the vehicle’s high price, recalls and public association with Musk all contributed to its decline; that is the publication’s interpretation, not a finding established by the sales figures alone.

perspectives.body: The Verge frames the Cybertruck’s fall as both a commercial failure and a political symbol tied to Musk. That broader interpretation goes beyond Tesla’s stated reason for freeing factory capacity for its robotaxi.

content.headline: Can AI cut heating bills? One two-year home test found lower gas use
content.shortHeadline: A two-year home test found AI heating controls used less gas
content.standfirst: A journalist’s comparison found that room-by-room smart controls used 18% less gas than his previous manual setup while keeping the house warmer. The result comes from one home and is not a guarantee of savings elsewhere.

image.caption: Smart radiator controls are part of the heating system tested.

sources.originalTitle: Can AI really save you money on your heating bill? I spent two years testing to find out

segments.body: Over two winters, a Guardian journalist compared a basic heating schedule and manual radiator controls with a Tado system that managed rooms individually and used automated features. After adjusting for hot-water use and comparing similar 213-day periods, the AI-controlled setup used 11,735.7 kilowatt hours of gas, against 14,316.7 kWh under manual control: 18% less in this home.

segments.title: A single-home result
segments.body: The journalist says the automated system also kept the house more comfortable, and estimated a £205.70 saving at the energy price cap then in effect. The setup cost about £930 in the test, with an optional subscription for AI features. This was one household’s comparison, using its particular home, heating equipment and schedule; the result does not establish typical savings for other homes.

content.headline: Anthropic used AI to accelerate its own research, METR finds, but redacted much
content.shortHeadline: METR finds AI sped up Anthropic research, but much evidence is red
content.standfirst: A restricted assessment found that AI contributed to faster progress at Anthropic, with employees reporting large productivity gains. Extensive redactions limit what the public can independently judge.

sources.originalTitle: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers

segments.body: An assessment by AI safety organisation METR found that Anthropic’s models improved roughly twice as quickly as a year earlier, and concluded that AI was responsible for most of the acceleration by October. Employees using the company’s most capable internal model reported being around 12 times as productive on average. METR said much of the work still involved AI assisting human researchers, rather than fully autonomous research.

segments.title: Evidence kept from public view
segments.body: Anthropic gave METR access to internal information but was allowed to redact the public report; METR said a majority of the evidence it considered most informative was removed and that some data requests were denied. Anthropic co-founder Sam McCandlish said the company withheld details for commercial reasons and to avoid giving rivals a roadmap. The limits make it harder for outsiders to assess both the findings and their uncertainties.

segments.title: Questions about oversight
segments.body: The findings have renewed debate about whether a company that advocates caution is accelerating AI development itself, and whether independent evaluators need more access. METR’s work concerns Anthropic and does not establish that AI can independently design successor systems. Researchers quoted in the report disagree about the implications, while some call for stronger public oversight.

content.headline: AI hacking tool exposed on hundreds of internet-facing servers
content.shortHeadline: Hundreds of exposed servers hosted an AI hacking tool
content.standfirst: Researchers found more than 800 publicly accessible deployments of Artex, an autonomous penetration-testing tool linked to cyberattacks. They say not every exposed instance is malicious, but the exposure could let outsiders access powerful tools.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web
AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?

segments.body: Cybersecurity firm Censys identified more than 800 Artex deployments accessible over the internet without a password. The open-source tool automatically probes systems for weaknesses and has been linked by security companies to attacks on South Korean financial firms and other organisations. Censys says it is unclear why so many deployments were publicly reachable and notes that some may be used for authorised testing.

segments.title: The defence gap
segments.body: The report says attackers have used Artex to exploit basic weaknesses such as weak passwords and missing multi-factor authentication. A cybersecurity expert interviewed by The Verge argues that AI can make it cheaper to find and exploit vulnerabilities, while effective defence remains costly and complex. That is his assessment; the reporting does not establish that every exposed instance has been used in an attack.

perspectives.body: Cognition security chief Alex Stamos argues that AI may lower the cost of offensive cyber operations faster than it lowers defensive costs. He calls for cheaper automated defence, but cautions against giving security agents unrestricted authority.

content.headline: AI impersonation scam used a British journalist’s byline in Science
content.shortHeadline: AI scam used journalist’s identity for a Science article
content.standfirst: A freelance journalist says someone pitched work in her name and a disputed article appeared under her byline. The journal removed it and says it has changed checks for new writers; the person who submitted the piece denies impersonation.

image.caption: Caroline Williams says a disputed article was published under her byline without her having written it.

sources.originalTitle: My identity was stolen by an AI scammer. It could happen to anyone

segments.body: Caroline Williams, a British journalist who writes about interoception, says she discovered that Science had published an article under her name that she had not written. The journal said it paid the submitter $1,000 for the piece, which it later removed. Science said an AI-detection tool flagged the first draft as AI-written and that it contained quotes copied from other articles.

segments.title: Conflicting accounts
segments.body: Williams says the submitter had approached other editors using an email address unlike her own and links to her previous work. The person told the i Paper they were a different journalist with the same name and had not intended to present Williams’s work as theirs; Science’s managing news editor said the pitch clearly identified the UK journalist. Science says it will speak with new writers and use detection software, while Williams fears similar pitches may damage freelancers’ reputations.

content.headline: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant helped with substitutions but nearly spoiled a cake
content.shortHeadline: A cooking app’s AI helped with swaps, but muddled a cake recipe
content.standfirst: In a hands-on test, an AI recipe assistant suggested workable ingredient changes and scaled a cake into muffins. It also gave the wrong butter quantity when the reviewer switched between recipe versions, making human checks essential.

sources.originalTitle: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake

segments.body: A Verge reviewer tested NYT Cooking’s AI assistant on ingredient substitutions, recipe scaling and equipment changes. It adapted a chicken-and-rice recipe to use ingredients on hand and gave useful suggestions for other dishes. The reviewer found the modified chicken recipe successful, but the test reflects one person’s experience rather than a systematic assessment of recipe safety or accuracy.

segments.title: Check the version
segments.body: The clearest failure came while baking: after the reviewer switched between the original Bundt cake and an AI-modified muffin recipe, the assistant gave the smaller recipe’s butter quantity without saying which version it meant. The reviewer says that amount would have made the original cake dry. The tool leaves the original recipe unchanged, but its versions can be confusing; the reviewer recommends checking quantities and timings against the source recipe.

content.headline: Geoffrey Hinton warns the AI race is outpacing control, while pointing to its
content.shortHeadline: Hinton warns of AI risks but says the technology could help
content.standfirst: The Nobel laureate argues that competition to build more capable systems is moving too quickly, while also describing possible benefits such as new materials and better batteries. These are his views, not settled predictions.

image.caption: An illustration of Geoffrey Hinton, who warns of AI risks while discussing its potential benefits.

sources.originalTitle: Godfather of AI warns humanity: It’s all hurtling out of control

segments.body: Geoffrey Hinton says competition among companies and countries to make AI more capable is proceeding without enough work on how to keep systems beneficial to people. He believes AI could surpass human intelligence, but stresses uncertainty over when that might happen. He also argues that a simple shutdown switch may not be sufficient if a system can persuade people not to use it.

segments.title: Risks and possible gains
segments.body: Hinton says AI could help develop materials, including improved batteries that might make it easier to store renewable energy, and could increase productivity. He also questions how any resulting wealth would be shared and argues that AI should be developed to serve people. His predictions about superintelligence and his proposed safeguards are his own analysis; the interview does not provide independent evidence that those outcomes are certain.

content.headline: AI-staged property photos leave renters and buyers feeling misled
content.shortHeadline: Renters say AI-staged property photos mislead them
content.standfirst: People who viewed homes after seeing furnished online images say the real properties were bare or run-down. Agents argue virtual staging can help people picture a space and save money, while Rightmove says misleading images can be removed.

image.caption: AI-generated furniture has been added to this property image; the BBC identifies it as an example of virtual staging.

sources.originalTitle: AI in property listings is false advertising, house-hunters say

segments.body: Renters and buyers told the BBC they felt misled by property listings showing furniture and finishes that were not present when they visited. One prospective buyer said a flat advertised with a modern interior was in disrepair; a renter said only two of a dozen viewed properties matched the furnishings shown. The BBC says some listings were labelled as virtually staged or enhanced, while others were not.

segments.title: Disclosure matters
segments.body: Estate agents cited the cost of physical staging and said virtual furniture can help viewers understand room scale. Rightmove says AI-generated imagery is permitted when clearly labelled and that agents are responsible for what they upload; it says it can require amendments or remove misleading listings. The reporting shows disagreement about whether staging helps viewers or creates false expectations, not that all AI-enhanced listings are undisclosed.

content.headline: UK research hub plans AI-supported dementia clinics from 2029
content.shortHeadline: UK project plans AI-supported dementia clinics from 2029
content.standfirst: A six-year research hub backed by £10m in public funding and a further £10m from partners plans to combine scans, genetics, blood markers and cognitive tests. Its targets are ambitions, not demonstrated clinical results.

image.caption: The project plans to combine brain scans, blood biomarkers, genetics and health data to support dementia assessment.

sources.originalTitle: Multimillion-pound project to detect dementia

segments.body: The University of Exeter-led BRAINIAC Hub plans to bring together 11 universities and 10 NHS sites to study dementia diagnosis, prevention and treatment. The six-year project has £10m from the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council, with another £10m expected from industry, charity and NHS partners. The first clinics are planned for 2029, initially for people referred through the NHS.

segments.title: Targets still to be tested
segments.body: The project intends to combine brain imaging, genetics, blood biomarkers and digital cognitive tests with AI to build a picture of brain health. Its stated aims include faster assessment and earlier identification of risk. These are project goals, not evidence that the system can yet diagnose dementia earlier or improve outcomes. The university says the clinics will be designed with patients and clinicians.

content.headline: US chip approvals raise questions after Nvidia supplier’s China office appears
content.shortHeadline: Report questions US approval of Nvidia chip buyers in China
content.standfirst: The Verge reports that a Chinese company cleared to handle Nvidia H200 chips had an apparently empty office and links to a blacklisted investment firm. The account raises questions about checks on approved buyers, but does not establish that the company received chips.

sources.originalTitle: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China

segments.body: The Verge, citing the New York Times, reports that New Matrix, a Chinese company on a list of firms approved to handle Nvidia H200 chips, had an empty-looking office and little visible evidence of active operations. The report says the company’s owners have ties to a Chinese private-equity firm blacklisted by the US government in 2024.

segments.title: Questions over oversight
segments.body: The reporting raises questions about how companies are vetted for access to advanced AI chips and whether approvals have included firms connected to restricted entities. It does not establish that New Matrix received chips or that the Commerce Department or Nvidia knowingly violated rules. The article says US restrictions on sales to China were relaxed under the Trump administration after Nvidia agreed to give the government a share of sales.
